desc:
In the m x n grid, all values are distinct. A cell is a peak if its value is strictly greater than the values of all its existing neighbours (up, down, left and right; cells outside the grid do not count).

The grid is guaranteed to contain exactly one peak. Return its position as [row, col]. A solution that inspects far fewer than m * n cells exists: aim for O(m log n) time.

For example, in [[10, 20, 15], [21, 30, 14], [7, 16, 12]] only the cell holding 30 is a peak, so the answer is [1, 1].
constraints: The grid contains exactly one peak cell
hints: Checking every cell for being larger than its neighbours is O(m * n). In 1D you can binary search for a peak by following the larger neighbour. Can the same idea work on columns?
Take the middle column and find the row of its maximum. Compare that cell with its left and right neighbours. If it beats both, it is a peak.

If the left neighbour is bigger, a peak must exist in the columns to the left of the middle (discard the middle column and everything to its right); if the right neighbour is bigger, search to the right. Repeat on the shrinking column range.
editorial: Walking uphill never gets stuck in a corner: from any cell, moving to a larger neighbour repeatedly must end in a peak, because the values are finite and strictly increase along the walk. The binary search uses this to throw away half of the columns each step.

Look at the middle column mid and take the row r where that column is largest. Call the cell X = grid[r][mid]. Its up and down neighbours are smaller than X by the choice of r. If its left and right neighbours are also smaller, X is a peak. Otherwise one side holds a larger neighbour, say the left one. Walking uphill from that neighbour can never cross column mid, because to enter column mid it would have to pass through a cell larger than the neighbour, and every cell of that column is at most X, which is smaller than the neighbour. Hence a peak exists in the columns left of mid. The same argument works on the right.

Each step halves the columns and costs O(m) to find the column maximum, so the total is O(m log n) time and O(1) space. The problem statement promises a single peak, which only makes the answer unique; the algorithm itself finds some peak of any grid with distinct neighbouring values.
solution:
def gridPeak(grid):
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    lo, hi = 0, n - 1
    NEG = float("-inf")
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        r = max(range(m), key=lambda i: grid[i][mid])
        v = grid[r][mid]
        left = grid[r][mid - 1] if mid > 0 else NEG
        right = grid[r][mid + 1] if mid < n - 1 else NEG
        if v > left and v > right:
            return [r, mid]
        if left > v:
            hi = mid - 1
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return [-1, -1]
